cards.prompt: Walk through TCP's three-way handshake. Why does each side pick a random initial sequence number?

keyPoints.text: The client does an active open; the server has already done a passive open (LISTEN)
1: client sends SYN with its initial sequence number x
2: server replies with one segment carrying both SYN (its own sequence number y) and ACK = x + 1
3: client sends ACK = y + 1
The ACK field names the next sequence number expected, which implicitly acknowledges everything before it
Timers on the first two segments trigger retransmission if no reply arrives

Random initial sequence numbers keep two incarnations of the same connection from reusing the same sequence numbers too soon, while a segment from the earlier incarnation could still interfere with the later one

cards.explanation: The handshake is how the two sides agree on parameters, here the starting sequence numbers for each direction's byte stream. Data flows only after setup completes.

cards.prompt: How does TCP close a connection, and why does the side that closes first wait in TIME_WAIT?

keyPoints.text: Setup is asymmetric (active vs passive open) but teardown is symmetric: each side closes its own direction independently
One side can close (no more sending) while the other keeps sending on its half
Closing first: ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED
Other side closing first: ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED
TIME_WAIT lasts twice the maximum IP datagram lifetime (120 seconds)
Reason: the final ACK to the peer's FIN might be lost, so the peer may retransmit its FIN; a delayed FIN could otherwise tear down a new connection reusing the same ports

cards.explanation: A third path exists when both sides close at the same time: ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → CLOSING → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED.

cards.prompt: How does TCP flow control keep a fast sender from overrunning a slow receiver?

keyPoints.text: TCP's sliding window gives reliable delivery, in-order delivery, and flow control
The receiver advertises a window (AdvertisedWindow header field) sized to its free buffer space
The sender keeps unacknowledged data (LastByteSent − LastByteAcked) at or below AdvertisedWindow
EffectiveWindow = AdvertisedWindow − (LastByteSent − LastByteAcked); the sender can send only while it's above 0
If the receiving app reads slowly, the advertised window shrinks with each segment, down to 0, which stops the sender
On the send side, TCP blocks the writing app when the send buffer is full

cards.explanation: This is how a slow receiving process ends up stopping a fast sending process: its buffer fills, the advertised window hits zero, and back-pressure propagates to the sender's application.

cards.prompt: Explain TCP's additive increase / multiplicative decrease. Why cut fast and grow slowly?

keyPoints.text: The sender keeps a CongestionWindow; the max in flight is min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow)
No one tells the sender the right congestion window; it infers congestion from the network
A timeout is read as congestion, because packets are rarely lost to transmission errors
Multiplicative decrease: on each timeout, halve the window, but never below one packet (MSS)
Additive increase: grow by about one packet per RTT, done as a fraction (MSS/CongestionWindow) per ACK
Over time the window traces a sawtooth
Cut fast because too large a window compounds: dropped packets get retransmitted and make congestion worse

cards.explanation: AIMD is described as a necessary condition for a congestion-control mechanism to be stable, in contrast to additive increase/additive decrease.

cards.prompt: What is TCP slow start, and how does it combine with additive increase after a loss?

keyPoints.text: Additive increase is too slow to ramp up a connection from a cold start
Slow start begins with a congestion window of one packet and adds one packet per ACK
That doubles the packets in flight every RTT: exponential, not linear, growth
After a timeout, CongestionThreshold is set to the halved window and the window is reset to one packet
Slow start runs until the window reaches CongestionThreshold, then additive increase takes over (one packet per RTT)

cards.explanation: Despite its name, slow start grows the window quickly. It's "slow" only compared with dumping a whole advertised window onto the network at once.

cards.prompt: How do fast retransmit and fast recovery work, and what do they improve?

keyPoints.text: The receiver ACKs every arriving packet; an out-of-order packet triggers a duplicate of the last ACK
Duplicate ACKs suggest an earlier packet was lost (or only delayed)
After three duplicate ACKs, the sender retransmits the missing packet without waiting for a timeout
It adds to timeouts rather than replacing them; with small windows there aren't enough packets in flight to produce duplicate ACKs
It removes about half of coarse-grained timeouts, for roughly 20% more throughput
Fast recovery: instead of dropping to one packet and running slow start, use the ACKs still in the pipe to clock sending

cards.explanation: When the retransmitted packet arrives, the receiver sends one cumulative ACK covering everything it has buffered since.

cards.prompt: Define dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantom reads, and serialization anomalies. What does Serializable guarantee?

keyPoints.text: Dirty read: reading data written by a concurrent transaction that hasn't committed
Nonrepeatable read: re-reading data you read earlier and finding another transaction modified it (and committed since the first read)
Phantom read: re-running a query and finding the set of matching rows changed because of another committed transaction
Serialization anomaly: the result of committing a group of transactions matches no one-at-a-time ordering of them
Serializable: concurrent execution has the same effect as running the transactions one at a time in some order, so none of these can happen

cards.explanation: The SQL standard defines the three weaker levels by which of these phenomena they must prevent.

cards.prompt: Compare Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable, using PostgreSQL's behavior as the example.

keyPoints.text: Read Uncommitted is allowed to show dirty reads in the standard, but in PostgreSQL it behaves like Read Committed
Read Committed (PostgreSQL's default): each statement sees a snapshot as of when that statement started, so two SELECTs in one transaction can differ
Read Committed allows nonrepeatable reads, phantoms, and serialization anomalies
Repeatable Read: the snapshot is taken at the start of the transaction's first non-transaction-control statement, so successive SELECTs see the same data
PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read also prevents phantom reads; only serialization anomalies remain possible
Repeatable Read and Serializable apps must be ready to retry on serialization failures
Serializable prevents all four phenomena

cards.explanation: Read Committed works well for simple updates to predetermined rows (like adjusting one account balance) but can give inconsistent results for commands with complex search conditions.
